observed: GET /design/{id}/explanation re-queues the explain task forever. The route's staleness branch fires whenever the task is not ready and the design is older than 300 s, and it re-queues with the SAME deterministic task id. The stored explanation is only written when the poll observes status 'written', so a slow task is re-queued on every poll, and each re-queue overwrites the previous one, so the loop never ends.
expected: A design is explained once. A slow or lost task is retried at most once, and a retry that would race the running task does not. Every design costs one model call, not N.
evidence: celery log: 15 'received' and 14 'succeeded' for explain_design[explain-010db3ec-...-v1] (one design), 10/10 for explain-a4df3bb8-..., 2/2 for explain-82a1b4b2-...; each cycle 45-90 s of model time
verified_by: tests/test_explanation_queue.py (18 tests) and tests/test_migrations.py (6 tests). 2748 passed, 13 skipped.

observed: A diode fitted the wrong way round is invisible to the verifier, on a board where the second source RESOLVES. Seeded on the real load_switch output (D1 = 1N4148W-7-F, SOD-123): the anode and cathode are transposed. The verifier's IV.2 check actually runs on this part â€” part_pinouts.lookup('1N4148W-7-F', 'SOD-123') resolves by prefix to KiCad's Diode:1N4148W, whose symbol says pad 1 = K and pad 2 = A â€” and it reports '3 part(s) agree with an independent transcription (T1)'. No check changes status between the clean board and the defective one. The board is emitted for fabrication. The mechanism is architectural: compile_board calls verify_board(board, netlist) with the SAME netlist it just compiled from, so the verifier can only answer 'is this board what I was told to build', never 'is what I was told to build right'. IV.2 compares the symbol's terminals to the board's pads; it never asks which NET belongs on which terminal, because a symbol says nothing about that and only the circuit does.
expected: A check that compares a part's pin-to-net map against the DESIGN INTENT, and a design intent that survives into the verifier. For a diode that means reading the polarity against the requirement: the cathode on the rail, so the diode is reverse biased in steady state and conducts only while the load's inductance collapses. A wrong pinout is a critical-class defect with no check behind it today (the same gap as F-S0-0001 and F-0007, but here the symbol lookup is NOT the reason).
evidence: tests/fixtures/alpha_known_bad/reversed_diode/ (mutate.py, manifest.json, board_base.json, board_defective.json, netlist_base.json, netlist_defective.json); the mutator's own run prints 'no check changed' and the gate says {emit: true}. backend/pcb_engine/verify.py IV.2 (lines 875-960) and compile_board.py line 223.

observed: Every timestamp the ORM wrote used datetime.utcnow(), which returns the UTC wall clock with NO tzinfo. asyncpg reads a naive datetime as LOCAL time, so on a host 5.5 hours off UTC the row landed 5.5 hours in the past. Measured against the live database: writing 15:21:10 naive produced a stored value of 09:51:10+00, an age of 5:30:00. The explanation route compares a design's age against a 300 s staleness window, so a design two seconds old looked five and a half hours old. The route concluded the attempt had been lost and fired its one allowed retry on the VERY FIRST poll, then reported 'unavailable - the queue is not delivering tasks (is a Celery worker running?)' while a worker was running and answering. The F-0006 cap did hold the attempts at 2, so the runaway loop was gone, but the retry was spurious and the status was wrong for 38 s. The repository's own tests missed it because their fake ledger builds timezone-aware datetimes by hand; the real database never did. The Docker image is UTC and behaves correctly, which is why CI is green.
expected: Timestamps written into a timestamptz column carry their offset. Aware UTC everywhere, so a row means the same instant on every host. The age arithmetic in the explanation route also has to survive a naive value coming back from a row written by an older build.
evidence: tests/test_utc_timestamps.py (10 tests; verified to FAIL when the naive calls are put back). Live measurement against the running PostgreSQL: naive 15:21:10 stored as 09:51:10+00, age 5:30:00.000333. backend/db/models.py (14 column defaults) and backend/db/crud.py (10 explicit writes) both now use an aware UTC. Blast radius beyond the explanation route: every age comparison on a stored timestamp, including api/routes/firmware.py's build-age check.

Reproduced the lookup half: part_pinouts.lookup('2N2222A','TO-92') -> "no KiCad symbol is named for '2N2222A'". The KiCad 10 index has PN2222A, MMBT2222A, PMBT2222A, PZT2222A, FFB2222A, but no 2N2222A. Exact match misses, and the prefix rule (:313) needs want.startswith(base), which '2N2222A' vs 'PN2222A' fails. That is correct behaviour: name bridging would be the TO-92 trap. Defect 1 is a data gap, not a matcher bug. Defect 2 is the real one: _check_part_pinouts files the part under 'unchecked' and returns IV.2 status 'unknown' ('no part could be compared') plus IV.2b 'unknown'. Report.gate (:119-125) refuses only on failed() findings, so unknown never blocks; gate().emit stays True and ok=True. compile_board.py:237 then returns verified:true. Plan decision 9 (implementation plan :145) says an unknown pinout blocks export; it is not implemented. Smallest fix: (a) Report.gate refuses emit when IV.2b lists any non-symmetric part (unknown pinout = REFUSED, or at most 'EMITTED WITH RESIDUALS' with no fab files), with a test from the swapped_pins calibration case; (b) for the lookup gap, add an explicit, page-cited override table keyed on (orderable MPN, package) -> pin map (e.g. 2N2222A TO-92 E-B-C per the maker's datasheet, cited), consulted before the KiCad index, never a name alias. Never bridge 2N2222A to PN2222A/P2N2222A by name.

Correction to my diagnosis: the example "2N2222A TO-92 E-B-C" is not a fact to copy. TO-92 2N2222A pin order differs by maker (some E-B-C, onsemi P2N2222A C-B-E). The override row must be keyed on the exact maker part number and cite that maker datasheet page; no pin order is implied by my note.
